challenging_evidence.finding: The figure circulating publicly is worded as 'cycling trips'. CBC reported 'Nearly 1.3 million cycling trips have happened in Edmonton through the first seven months of 2026, according to bike counter data.' The City's dataset does not use the word trips; it publishes counts of passages past fixed points. One person riding to work and home past the same counter is two counts; one journey past two counters is two counts; a rider where there is no counter is none. The number is therefore right and the noun is wrong.

claims.interpretation_notes:
MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN

What the brief defines. The brief fixes a coverage rule: a counter is classifiable only if it published bicycle counts for at least 20 of July 2025's 31 days, and 'If the verdict set is empty, any counter in it is not classifiable, or the City's locations data does not allow on-street lanes to be told from recreational paths, return Not established'.

Why it distorts. Exactly one counter in the verdict set falls short, and it falls short because the device died, not because the lane went unmeasured. 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue recorded 4,944 cyclists over the 30 days of June 2025, about 165 a day. In July it published 16 days whose daily counts decay from 99 on 1 July to 0 on 13-16 July, and then it stopped publishing forever: its last record in the dataset is 2025-07-16T23:45:00 and it appears nowhere in 2026. That is a failure signature. Under the brief's rule this one dead sensor voids the verdict for the whole set, and the panel returns Not established, which a reader will read as 'the record cannot tell us'. The record tells us a great deal: the other twenty metered on-street counters have July 2025 median daily bicycle counts from 46 to 979, with a median of 222.5, and nineteen of the twenty are at or above 50 a day. Not established is not a fair description of that record.

What framing I would use instead. Keep the 20-day rule, and add: where a counter misses the threshold because its published series terminates or decays to zero and does not resume, classify it on the nearest complete month inside the riding season (here June 2025, median about 165 a day) and say so; or exclude it, name the exclusion, and report the verdict both with and without it. Either fix leaves the verdict definition-sensitive between Contradicted and Partially supported, which is an honest result; the present rule replaces an answer with a non-answer on the strength of a broken sensor.

Answering the claim as posed. The verdict below is Not established, as the brief requires. For the record, had the rule permitted the twenty classifiable counters to carry it: at the primary cutoff of 25 a day no counter is below it, which is Contradicted; at the alternative cutoff of 50 a day one counter is below it (96 Street S of Jasper Avenue, median 46) and nineteen are at or above it, which is Partially supported. If the failed counter's 16 available July days were used at face value (median 3), the primary cutoff would give Partially supported. So the failed counter genuinely straddles two verdicts, which is why the brief's rule is not arbitrary, and why the fix has to be to resolve the counter rather than to drop the rule.

A second, smaller definitional point, reported not raised: the City's counter-locations dataset py7x-4d39 publishes only a description, a counter configuration and coordinates. It has no facility-type field, so it does not by itself tell an on-street lane from a recreational path. I classified each counter from its description (names containing SUP, Trail, Ravine, Park, Bridge, or a park name read as off-street; names of the form 'street X of street' read as on-street), cross-checked against the vocabulary in the City's separate Bike Routes dataset vd4b-a4iv, which does classify facilities as ON ROAD / OFF ROAD and as Protected Bike Lane, Painted Bike Lane, Shared Pathway and so on. The classification is mine. A strict reading of the brief's third trigger ('the City's locations data does not allow on-street lanes to be told from recreational paths') would return Not established on that ground too.

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than about 2 percent of Edmonton's population rides a bicycle, tested as the share of Edmonton residents who rode a bicycle at least once in the twelve months before a representative instrument's reference date.
claims.interpretation_notes: The brief's editor recorded that no representative Edmonton twelve-month cycling-participation measure was identified and invited reviewers to correct that. I identified one, so on the brief's own terms it carries the verdict and the editor's note is wrong. The Alberta Recreation Survey is a random-sample survey of Albertans run roughly every four to five years, with the City of Edmonton among its funders since at least 2013. Its participation question asks 'Which of the following activities did you personally take part in during the past 12 months?' with 'Bicycling' as one option, which is the twelve-month window the brief fixes and the participation measure the brief asks for. The published reports give Alberta-wide figures only, but the Government of Alberta publishes the respondent-level data files on its open data portal, and those files carry a city identifier: 'city_flag' with a '(1) Edmonton' category in 2022, 'region_num' with '(2) Edmonton' in 2017, and a region code 1 with n=593 in 2013, matching the n=593 the 2013 report gives for its Edmonton stratum. The Edmonton shares below are my calculations from those published files; I validated the method by recomputing the Alberta-wide 2013 respondent figure and getting 42.3 per cent, exactly what the report prints. On the primary threshold P is 43.5 per cent, far above the 5.0 per cent Contradicted line, and equally far above the 6.0 per cent alternative line, so both cutoff sets return Contradicted and the finding is not definition-sensitive. The two lane-use wordings in the merge, '.001% of the population' and '500 people using the bike lanes 4 months of the year', are reported in limitations as made and unmeasured; no participation figure is set against them.

supporting_evidence.finding: The Canadian Community Health Survey, the instrument the brief names as a candidate, was ruled out on both geography and reference period. Its bicycling questions ask about the past three months, not twelve, they were discontinued after the 2013/14 cycle, and the published analysis is national: 23.3 per cent of the 28,887,405 Canadians represented reported bicycling for leisure and/or to get to work or school in the previous three months. No Edmonton or Alberta figure is published in it.

limitations: The Alberta Recreation Survey covers adults aged 18 and over. Children are outside its denominator, and the claim's own denominator is the whole population. Children and teenagers cycle more than adults, not less, so an all-ages figure would be higher, not lower.

The Edmonton shares are my calculations from published respondent-level files, not figures the published reports print. The reports publish Alberta-wide results only. I show the arithmetic: 325/747 for 2022, 199/578 and 199/539 for 2017, 234/593 for 2013.

The 2022 file's city_flag identifies City of Edmonton respondents; the 2013 report describes its strata as 'Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, and rest of Alberta' without spelling out whether Edmonton means the municipality or the wider area. If the 2013 stratum is the region rather than the city, the 2013 figure is a regional alternative; the 2022 figure, which carries the verdict, is city-flagged.

The instrument counts anyone who bicycled at least once in a year. It says nothing about how often, and it counts a bicycle by the respondent's own understanding; there is no definition of bicycle in the question.

Response bias runs against the claim's opponents, not for them: the 2013 report warns of 'a relatively higher proportion of older residents' opinions in the final sample', and the 2022 report says very few Albertans aged 18 to 34 completed the survey. Both skews would depress measured cycling, so 43.5 per cent is if anything conservative.

A shorter-period figure, required as a qualification: the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey recorded 54,800 bicycle trips among 3,139,100 daily weekday trips by City residents, that is 1.7 per cent of trips on a single fall weekday. The share of people who ride in a year and the share of trips made by bicycle on one weekday are different numbers over different denominators, and this claim is the first.

Two captured wordings in this claim's merge are about people using the bike lanes rather than about people who ride: 'bike lanes for the .001% of the population' and '500 people using the bike lanes 4 months of the year'. They were made, and nothing published in Edmonton measures the distinct residents who use bike lanes. No participation figure is set against them here, in either direction.

No census-metropolitan-area equivalent is published for this measure, so the required CMA alternative cannot be given. The nearest published alternatives are Alberta-wide: 49 per cent in 2022, 46 per cent in 2017.

claims.suggested_short_answer: No. The figure being passed around is out by more than an order of magnitude, and the reason is that it is answering a different question. In the 2022 Alberta Recreation Survey, a random-sample survey the City of Edmonton helped fund, 325 of 747 Edmonton respondents said they had bicycled in the past twelve months. That is 43.5 per cent, or 50 per cent once the survey's own city weights are applied. The 2017 and 2013 cycles put it at about 34 and 40 per cent. The one and two per cent figures in circulation are commuting and trip shares, which count something else entirely: how many journeys are made by bike, not how many people own and ride one. Both numbers can be true at once.

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than 1 percent of Edmonton's population rides a bicycle year-round, and fewer than 15 percent ride in the rest of the year, both parts to come from one instrument and one representative Edmonton sample with a seasonal split.
claims.interpretation_notes: The holder wrote 'use them year round', where 'them' is the bike lanes. No published Edmonton instrument measures the distinct residents who use bike lanes in any season, so the proposition tests riding a bicycle instead. That substitution is open, it is stated in limitations, and nothing here may be described as a finding about lane use. I searched independently and did not identify any representative Edmonton instrument that publishes both a year-round and a non-winter cycling share from one sample. The Alberta Recreation Survey, which does carry the verdict on claim 3, asks about the past twelve months with no seasonal split at all; I checked its 2022 respondent-level file for any season, winter, summer or frequency variable attached to activities and found only 'how many times did you participate' for the respondent's three favourite activities. The one Edmonton instrument that does split the year is the City's Edmonton Insight Community, an opt-in online panel, which the brief says cannot carry the verdict and which I report under its own name below. So the verdict is Not established. Reachability check: both parts had a defined threshold and either could have held; the outcome turns on the absence of an instrument, not on the numbers.

supporting_evidence.finding: The Alberta Recreation Survey, the only representative-sample instrument I found that measures Edmonton cycling participation, has no seasonal split. Its participation question is 'Which of the following activities did you personally take part in during the past 12 months?', a single annual window. Its frequency question applies only to the respondent's three favourite activities and asks for a count of times per year, not a season. It cannot produce Part A or Part B.

challenging_evidence.finding: A panel figure, reported under its own name and carrying no verdict. The City's Edmonton Insight Community mixed-topic survey of 19-25 August 2014, 816 respondents, asked bike ridership twice, once generally and once for winter. Winter: 715 of 816, that is 87.6 per cent, answered 'Never ride a bike'; the remaining 12.4 per cent reported riding in winter daily (1.0 per cent), four or more times a week (1.6), two to three times a week (1.7), once a week (2.8) or once a month (5.3). General: 40.1 per cent never, 59.9 per cent at some frequency. Read at face value that panel would put Part A at about 12 per cent against a 2 per cent ceiling and Part B at about 60 per cent against a 15 per cent ceiling, so both parts would fail. It is an opt-in panel and the brief forbids it carrying the verdict, and cyclists are exactly the people most likely to opt into a bike survey.

claims.proposition_evaluated: About 2 percent of all trips in Edmonton are made by bicycle, that is bicycle trips as a share of all trips by City of Edmonton residents in the most recent Edmonton region household travel survey published by 2026-09-03.
claims.interpretation_notes: The most recent published Edmonton travel survey on the as-of date is the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey, fieldwork 14 September to 11 December 2015, summary report published April 2018. Its successor, Navigating Tomorrow, launched in 2025 and had published no results by the as-of date. The primary figure is for City of Edmonton residents: 1.7 per cent, numerator 54,800 bicycle trips, denominator 3,139,100 total daily trips, weekday, 24-hour travel day. That sits inside the primary Supported band of 1.5 to 2.5 per cent and inside the alternative Supported band of 1.2 to 3.0 per cent, so both cutoff sets return Supported and the finding is not definition-sensitive. The required regional alternative, reported under its own name, is 0.8 per cent for Region residents, numerator 10,600 bicycle trips, denominator 1,331,800; note that 'Region' in this survey means the surrounding municipalities, not Edmonton plus its region. The survey reports weekday trips only, which I say here rather than mixing day types.

The survey's date. A 2015 figure is eleven years old on the as-of date, and the intervening decade added the downtown protected bike lane network, the 132 Avenue and 119 Avenue facilities and much else. The direction of the trend inside the survey series is sharply upward: 0.4 per cent of City trips in 1994, 1.0 per cent in 2005, 1.7 per cent in 2015 (reviewer's calculation from Table 3-2).

The second half of the holder's sentence, 'although it's higher in neighborhoods with bike infrastructure', is reported and not tested. The survey publishes no neighbourhood-level mode share. It does publish sector-level bicycle trip volumes: 'The University sector has the greatest number of bicycling trips, followed by the Southeast Inner and Southwest Inner sectors. Together, these represent one-third of the bicycling trips recorded in the study area. Overall, 36% of all bicycling trips are made entirely within the same sector. Residents who live in or closer to the Central band are more likely to walk and cycle than those who live further away.' That is trip volume by sector, not mode share by neighbourhood, so it does not test the holder's sub-clause either way.

The other document the holder named, a Statistics Canada table on 'Main mode of commuting for the 10 largest census metropolitan areas', is a commuting table. Statistics Canada does publish main mode of commuting for census metropolitan areas from the 2021 Census, for instance table 98-10-0465-01. Whatever its exact identity, a commuting table counts journeys to work by the employed labour force; it does not measure trips. The holder cited a commuting source for a trips figure, and the trips figure happens to come from the other document he named.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Most cycling in Edmonton is recreational rather than commuting, tested as recreation trips as a share of all bicycle trips in the most recent published Edmonton region household travel survey, the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey.
claims.interpretation_notes: The 2015 survey does not publish bicycle trips broken down by purpose. It publishes the inverse cross-tabulation, Table 3-10, which gives each mode's share of each purpose, with the bicycle row rounded to whole percentages. The purpose split of bicycle trips has to be recovered from it, and I show the arithmetic below and label it my calculation. The survey's own purpose categories, verbatim, are: HB-Work, HB-PSE (post-secondary education), HB-School, HB-Shopping, HB-Social / Rec, HB-Personal Bus., HB-Pick up/Drop off, HB-Other, NHB-Work, NHB-Other, where HB is home-based and NHB non-home-based. I counted 'HB-Social / Rec' as recreational and 'HB-Work' plus 'NHB-Work' as commuting; the other six are third categories, which the brief's ladder expressly contemplates. The mapping is complete in the sense the ladder needs: every category is assigned to recreation, to commuting, or to neither, with none left ambiguous between recreation and commuting. On that mapping recreation is about 21 per cent of bicycle trips and commuting about 38 per cent, so commuting exceeds recreation and recreation is below 35 per cent. Both cutoff sets therefore return Contradicted. The finding is not definition-sensitive across the two ladders, but it is sensitive to the instrument, and that is where my confidence goes: see limitations. The 'usually within a short distance' half of the holders' wording is reported, not tested: the survey gives an average bicycle trip length of 4.1 km for City residents in 2015, against 9.4 km by car and 1.1 km on foot.

supporting_evidence.finding: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey, Table 3-10, City of Edmonton residents, bicycle share of each trip purpose: HB-Work 3 per cent of 650,700 trips; HB-PSE 3 per cent of 82,500; HB-School 2 per cent of 255,400; HB-Shopping 1 per cent of 352,600; HB-Social / Rec 3 per cent of 399,800; HB-Personal Bus. 1 per cent of 226,200; HB-Pick up/Drop off 1 per cent of 217,000; HB-Other 1 per cent of 172,100; NHB-Work 1 per cent of 185,800; NHB-Other 1 per cent of 597,000. Multiplying out gives about 11,994 recreational bicycle trips and about 21,379 commuting bicycle trips (19,521 home-based work plus 1,858 non-home-based work), against a derived total of 56,605 and a published bicycle total of 54,800. Recreation is about 21 per cent of bicycle trips, commuting about 38 per cent. Commuting exceeds recreation and recreation is below 35 per cent, so the claim fails on both ladders.

claims.suggested_short_answer: The one Edmonton instrument that can answer this says the opposite, and it has a blind spot. Working from the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey's purpose-by-mode table, about 21 per cent of bicycle trips by City residents were home-based social or recreational and about 38 per cent were work trips, so commuting outweighs recreation and the 'most cycling is recreational' claim fails on both of the brief's thresholds. But the survey recorded 24 hours of weekday travel between mid-September and mid-December, and recreational riding is exactly what concentrates on weekends and in summer. Nobody publishes an all-days, all-season purpose breakdown for Edmonton bicycle trips, so this is the answer the available instrument gives rather than the answer to the year. Alongside it, an opt-in City panel in 2014 found 87 per cent of riders naming recreation as a reason they ride and 42 per cent naming commuting, which counts reasons rather than trips and cannot measure a population. On the short-distance half of the claim, the average Edmonton bicycle trip in 2015 was 4.1 km against 9.4 km by car.
